summary: This Bitmovin developer blog post, written by Andrea Fassina on 10 March 2020, is a comprehensive guide to lossy compression algorithms for video developers. It explains why compression matters for content distribution, defines lossy compression as producing a close approximation rather than an exact copy, and covers distortion metrics such as perceptual distortion, mean square error and PSNR. It then describes the two-step process of quantization and transform coding, including DCT, wavelet and 2D Haar transforms. The page's navigation menus, product promotions and related-post listings are boilerplate and were ignored.
one_line: A 2020 Bitmovin developer guide explaining lossy compression algorithms, distortion metrics like PSNR, quantization, and transform coding such as DCT and wavelets.
key_facts: The article 'Lossy Compression Algorithms: Everything a Developer Needs to Know' was written by Andrea Fassina and dated 10 March 2020, with a 15 min read time.
Lossy compression means compressed data is not exactly the same as the original but a close approximation to it.
The note states that in most cases the human eye wouldn't even notice the difference between an original file and one compressed in a lossy way.
The note says lossy compression yields a much higher compression ratio than lossless compression, where an exact copy of the content is created.
The note states that if you have a high data rate and a zero distortion, it is a lossless compression scheme.
Peak-Signal-To-Noise Ratio (PSNR) is calculated by comparing the size of an error relative to the peak value of a signal, and is typically expressed in decibel units (dB).
The note says a good PSNR ratio will register values of around 80db.
The note states that quantization is the step that adds the most distortion in lossy compression.
The note lists three forms of quantization: uniform, non-uniform, and vector.
The note states that the DCT is lossless apart from rounding errors, and it splits the signal into a DC component and an AC component.
The note describes a wavelet transform as creating progressively smaller summary images, decreasing by a quarter of the size for each step.
The note describes 2D Haar Transform as the representation of a signal with a discrete non-differentiable (step) function, illustrated with an 8 x 8 image.
The note states that the human eye is less sensitive to higher spatial frequency components than lower spatial frequency components.
The note concludes that the goal of all compression algorithms is to achieve the highest possible compression ratio, with compression ratios coming down to cost and quality considerations.
